**Tentative project title:** 
Same Diagnosis, Different Bills? Variation in Hospital Charges and Estimated Costs for Five Common Conditions in New York, 2023

## Motivation
In New York, patients hospitalized for the same condition can receive very different bills depending on where they are treated, and we would like to describe this hospital variation. More recently, there was a lot of media buzz over surprise medical billing and an ongoing debate over hospital price transparency rules. We plan to use 2023 statewide discharge data for five common conditions (heart failure, major respiratory infections (after check mostly COVID-19), kidney and urinary tract infections, ischemic stroke, and sepsis) to look at three questions:

(1) How much did median charges and estimated costs vary across hospitals within each of the five conditions in 2023?

(2) How much of the between-hospital gap remains after accounting for severity of illness, age group, and length of stay?

(3) Are hospitals that are expensive for one condition also expensive for the others?

## Intended final products

* Exploratory data analyses of key variables
* Statistical report detailing methods & analyses, results, and discussion
* Webpage and 2-minute screencast describing our project

## Anticipated data sources

* Hospital Inpatient Discharges (SPARCS De-Identified): 2023, New York State Department of Health:
<https://health.data.ny.gov/Health/Hospital-Inpatient-Discharges-SPARCS-De-Identified/46xm-urtu/about_data>

* Health Facility General Information, New York State Department of Health:
<https://health.data.ny.gov/d/vn5v-hh5r>

## Planned analyses / visualizations / coding challenges

- **Analyses:** 
 * Compare hospital median charges and costs within each condition, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
 * Use a funnel plot of median cost against case volume to separate real outliers from small-sample noise.
 * Compute each hospital's charge-to-cost ratio to measure markup.
 * Fit regressions by condition to see how much hospital gaps shrink after adjusting for severity, age, and length of stay.
 * Use cross-validation to compare models with and without hospital, and linear vs. piecewise length of stay.
 * Check whether hospitals expensive for one condition are also expensive for the others.


- **Visualizations:** 
Hospital rankings for each condition, a charges vs. costs scatterplot, a heatmap comparing rankings across conditions (with gray cells where a hospital has too few cases), a hospital map, and a plotly dashboard.

- **Coding challenges and limitations:** 
The full dataset has 2.1 million rows, so we will download only what we need and reuse the same functions for all five conditions. 
Some columns need cleaning, and hospital IDs must be matched to a second dataset for locations. 
Charges and costs do not show what patients actually paid, and because the data are observational, we will not make causal claims.
